extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, propagandists, journalists, students of mass communication and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and executing modern propaganda/public-relations efforts: how to shape public opinion, organize groups, use media/authority figures, and ethically apply techniques to influence mass behavior. Draws on examples (fashion, wartime propaganda, charity drives) to illustrate tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious and intelligent manipulation of habits and opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: “THE conscious and intelligent manipulation of the organized habits and opinions of the masses is an important element in democratic society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda should be deliberate and thoughtful rather than accidental; practitioners constitute an 'invisible government' that shapes tastes, ideas, and conduct. Example: the public relations industry emerged to perform this conscious function after World War I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible government / use of opinion molders
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who manipulate the unseen mechanism of society constitute an invisible government which is the true ruling power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and work through persons with natural leadership, key social positions, or authority (editors, clergy, club leaders, presidents of organizations). These individuals often operate behind the scenes and can sway many followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing the field of choice for the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consents to have its choice narrowed to ideas and objects brought to its attention through propaganda of all kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-spot the most important issues and present a limited, practical set of options so the public can act without being overwhelmed by complexity. Use leaders and media to 'sift the data' and focus attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as necessary organization for free competition
rubrics_metrics.description: To make free competition function with reasonable smoothness, society permits free competition to be organized by leadership and propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use propaganda to coordinate market and social behavior (e.g., advertising fashions) so supply and demand can operate efficiently rather than chaos from individual testing/selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of modern propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: “Modern propaganda is a consistent, enduring effort to create or shape events to influence the relations of the public to an enterprise, idea or group.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective campaigns are sustained and systematic; they may create circumstances or images to alter public relations to the subject (product, policy, charity, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the anatomy of society (group structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The new propaganda takes account not merely of the individual, nor even of the mass mind alone, but also and especially of the anatomy of society, with its interlocking group formations and loyalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map social cleavages (social, political, economic, racial, religious, ethical) and identify the many subgroups and channels (clubs, professional bodies, periodicals, conventions) through which opinion flows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch a nerve at a sensitive spot (targeted appeals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Touch a nerve at a sensitive spot and you get an automatic response from certain specific members of the organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find and exploit specific motivations, prejudices, or desires within target groups to trigger predictable reactions (e.g., national pride, fashion aspiration, health concerns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure cooperation of group leaders and key men
rubrics_metrics.description: They secured the cooperation of the key men in every group—persons whose mere word carried authority to hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of followers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recruit and brief influential spokespeople whose endorsement will be transmitted through trusted channels to the larger group, rather than trying to persuade individuals directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances / manufacture events and pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a consistent effort to create or shape events... The practice of creating circumstances and of creating pictures in the minds of millions of persons is very common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage or engineer happenings, presentations, or visible examples (fashion placements, publicity events, endorsements) that make a desired idea appear natural or widespread—example: orchestrated velvet-fashion campaign in Paris and U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modern means of communication and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: With the printing press and the newspaper, the railroad, the telephone, telegraph, radio and airplanes, ideas can be spread rapidly and even instantaneously over the whole of America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit available mass-media channels (press, periodicals, radio, film, telegraph) to amplify messages; coordinate across media for rapid, wide dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage authoritative sources to lend credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An item 'made public by the State Department' or a Carnegie Foundation report is broadcast with all the authority of the institution so that the public would hear and believe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attach messages to respected institutions, official reports, or expert endorsements to increase acceptance. Example: using a foundation report or government release as the source of a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous and systematic effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The important thing is that it is universal and continuous; and in its sum total it is regimenting the public mind every bit as much as an army regiments the bodies of its soldiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustain campaigns over time rather than relying on one-off efforts; persistence builds stereotypes and mental clichés in the public mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit existing mental clichés and emotional habits
rubrics_metrics.description: They made use of the mental cliches and the emotional habits of the public to produce mass reactions against the alleged atrocities, the terror and the tyranny of the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame messages to align with preexisting beliefs, images, or emotional patterns to elicit stronger, faster responses; beware that this can also reinforce prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize and translate diffuse desires into political/actionable pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: A desire for a specific reform, however widespread, cannot be translated into action until it is made articulate, and until it has exerted sufficient pressure upon the proper law-making bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregate and concentrate diffuse public sentiment by organizing voices, creating focal events, and targeting relevant legislators or institutions to achieve policy outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligent minorities should lead propaganda efforts
rubrics_metrics.description: Only through the active energy of the intelligent few can the public at large become aware of and act upon new ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, organized, motivated groups—when guided by strategy—can shape majority opinion; plan leadership, messaging, and channels accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical constraint: truthfulness and public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda becomes vicious and reprehensible only when its authors consciously and deliberately disseminate what they know to be lies, or when they aim at effects which they know to be prejudicial to the common good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate cause merit and correctness of information; ethical practice distinguishes legitimate advocacy from deceitful propaganda. Use honesty and regard for public interests as boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use celebrities, spokesfigures and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: He ran huge campaigns for Chesterfield... You know all the techniques—models and movie stars with cigarettes coming out of their mouths... A popular actress was persuaded to wear the shoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy public figures, fashion leaders, and celebrities as exemplars to model behavior or consumption; visual and persona-based cues accelerate adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate upstream influencers and downstream media
rubrics_metrics.description: Its first function was to establish contact with the Lyons manufactories and the Paris couturiers... The American buyer or the American woman of fashion was simply shown the velvet creations in the atelier of the dressmaker or the milliner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with originators (designers, experts) to produce content or exemplars, then feed these to editors, reporters, and retailers so the idea cascades to consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map and exploit specialized publications/conventions/associations
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 22,128 periodical publications in America... The conventions scheduled for Cleveland... a fraction of the 5,500 conventions and rallies scheduled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify niche periodicals, trade journals, professional associations, and conventions relevant to a target segment and use them as focused distribution channels or recruitment grounds.
